short: This site's letter for how strong the evidence behind a health statement is: A (pooled human trials) down to E (laboratory only), or T for traditional use in an official monograph.
The exact thing a study tested: whole herb, a named extract, an essential oil, an isolated compound or a multi-herb formula. A grade belongs to its test article only.
A specific manufactured extract (solvent, plant-to-extract ratio, often a code name) used in a trial. Its results do not transfer automatically to other extracts or to tea.
Test article meaning the dried or fresh plant material itself (or a simple preparation of it), rather than an extract, oil or pure compound.
Test article meaning a single purified molecule (e.g. pure menthol), not the plant or an extract containing it.
Test article made of several plants combined (e.g. Sho-saiko-to, thyme + ivy syrup). Its evidence belongs to the combination, not to any one ingredient.
A study in which people are assigned by chance to the treatment or a comparison (often placebo), so that differences in outcome can be attributed to the treatment.
An inactive look-alike given to the comparison group of a trial, so that expectation effects are the same in both groups.
A trial in which each participant receives both the treatment and the comparison in turn, in random order, so each person is their own control.
A study in which everyone knows what treatment is being given; there is no blinding and often no control group. Graded C on this site.
A study that records what people already do or experience, without assigning a treatment. It can show association, not cause. Graded C here.
A published description of one patient (or a small series) with an unusual event, such as liver injury after a herbal product. Signals a possible harm; does not measure its risk.
A statistical pooling of the results of several studies of the same question, giving one overall estimate. Pooled human RCTs give grade A here.
A review that searches for every study on a question using stated methods and criteria, so the selection itself is not biased.
Studies in test tubes, dishes or isolated cells and receptors, outside a living organism. Graded E here and never phrased as an effect in people.
An experiment in living animals, usually rats or mice. Graded D here: it can show a mechanism or a hazard but is never phrased as an effect in people.
A use accepted by a regulator because a herb has been used safely that way for a long time (EMA: at least 30 years), not because trials proved it works. Graded T here.
EMA category for a herbal medicine whose efficacy and safety are supported by published scientific data, as opposed to traditional use alone.
The European Medicines Agency's Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products, which writes assessment reports and monographs on herbs and their constituents of concern.
An official summary of what a regulator or expert body accepts about a herb: indications, preparations, contraindications and warnings.
The official book of quality standards for medicines in Europe. It sets minimum contents, e.g. of thymol + carvacrol in thyme oil or of rosmarinic acid in lemon balm.
A free NIH database of drug- and supplement-induced liver injury, with case summaries and a likelihood score for each agent. The skullcap safety block draws on it.
Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry: separates the volatile molecules of an oil and identifies each by its mass spectrum. The source of most essential-oil percentages.
High-performance liquid chromatography: separates dissolved, non-volatile molecules such as rosmarinic acid or baicalin so they can be measured.
Area under the plasma concentration-time curve: the total exposure of the body to a drug. An interaction that lowers AUC means less drug reached the blood.
A regulator's figure for how much of a constituent of concern a person may be exposed to per day without special concern. A safety threshold, not a recommended amount.
Milligrams per kilogram of body weight: a dose scaled to the size of the person or animal.
Parts per million: 1 ppm is 1 mg per kg. 10,000 ppm = 1 %. Dr. Duke's reports most values in ppm, often without saying of what (leaf, oil or plant).
What an amount is 'per': fresh weight, dry weight, per cent of essential oil or per gram of extract. Values on different bases are never compared on this site.
Amount per gram of plant as harvested, water included. Fresh leaves are mostly water, so fresh-weight values are much lower than dry-weight values for the same plant.
Amount per gram of dried plant material. The usual basis for phenolics and flavonoids measured by HPLC.
An amount expressed as a share of the distilled oil, not of the plant. Thymol at 50 % of thyme oil may be well under 1 % of the dry leaf.
An amount relative to an extract after solvent removal. It depends on how much else the solvent pulled out, so it cannot be converted back to the plant.
One catalogue row saying that a compound was reported in a species' plant part, with amount, basis, source and a verified flag.
Whether the greenhouse entry's species is confirmed, needs checking, or is unresolved (skullcap: S. lateriflora or S. baicalensis?).
A molecule formed by handling rather than by the living plant, e.g. carnosol from carnosic acid on drying, chamazulene from matricin on steam distillation.
A cultivated variety selected and named by growers, e.g. 'Genovese' basil. Chemistry can differ sharply between cultivars of one species.
A rank below species for a distinct population, e.g. Origanum vulgare subsp. hirtum (Greek oregano). Databases do not always agree on subspecies.
The × in a name such as Mentha × piperita marks a hybrid: peppermint is a cross between water mint and spearmint.
A group of closely related species treated together under one name because they are hard to tell apart.
The scientific name a taxonomic authority currently recognises for a species; older names become synonyms (e.g. Rosmarinus officinalis is now Salvia rosmarinus).
The mint family: basil, mints, lemon balm, sage, rosemary, thyme, oregano and skullcap. Aromatic oils in surface glands; rosmarinic acid widespread.
The daisy family, including chamomile, ragweed and lettuce. Relevant here for allergy cross-reactivity.
Plants of the World Online, the Royal Botanic Gardens Kew database of accepted plant names; the source of accepted names and POWO ids here.
The Global Biodiversity Information Facility: an international species and occurrence database; its API supplied name matches and GBIF keys.
The numeric identifier of an organism in the NCBI Taxonomy database, used to link a plant to its gene and sequence records.
The compound identifier in PubChem, the NIH open chemistry database. Each compound record here links to its CID.
A fixed-length 27-character code computed from a structure, used to match the same molecule across databases.
A line of text that encodes a molecular structure (e.g. linalool: CC(=CCCC(C)(C=C)O)C). The site draws every structure from its SMILES.
Chemical Entities of Biological Interest: an ontology of small molecules; ChEBI ids link compounds to biological databases.
One of two mirror-image forms of a molecule. They can smell and act differently; basil linalool is usually reported as the (R)-(-) form.
The USDA database of plant chemicals compiled by James Duke; a source of occurrence rows, often in ppm with the plant part but not always the basis.
A Japanese database of species-metabolite relationships; used here to confirm that a compound has been reported from a species.
The natural-products occurrence database (lotus.naturalproducts.net) linking structures to the organisms they were reported from, with references.
A linear polymer of glucose that forms the load-bearing fibres of plant cell walls; the most abundant biopolymer on Earth.
Hemicelluloses and pectins: the branched and gel-forming polysaccharides that make up the hydrated matrix around cellulose in the primary cell wall.
A family of plant organelles (chloroplasts among them) with their own metabolism; the site of the MEP pathway to monoterpenes and diterpenes.
The fluid interior of the cell outside the organelles; the site of the mevalonate pathway to sesquiterpenes, sterols and triterpenes.
The stacked internal membranes of the chloroplast that carry chlorophyll and the complexes of the light reactions.
A large protein-pigment complex that captures light. Photosystem II splits water and releases oxygen; photosystem I helps make NADPH.
The two products of the light reactions: ATP, the cell's energy currency, and NADPH, its carrier of reducing power. Both pay for carbon fixation.
The enzyme that fixes CO2 into sugar in photosynthesis; slow, and confused by oxygen competing for its active site.
A compound not needed for basic growth that varies between lineages (terpenes, phenolics, alkaloids); plants use them in defence and signalling.
A tiny hair on the leaf surface that makes and stores essential oil. In the mints, oil sits in these glands, which is why rubbing the leaf releases the scent.
The plastid route that makes the C5 terpenoid building blocks (IPP/DMAPP) from pyruvate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate; feeds monoterpenes and diterpenes.
The cytosolic route from acetyl-CoA to the C5 terpenoid building blocks; feeds sesquiterpenes, sterols and triterpenes.
Isopentenyl diphosphate and dimethylallyl diphosphate: the two five-carbon units from which every terpenoid is assembled.
The ten-carbon precursor of every monoterpene; different terpene synthases fold it into menthol's, thymol's or camphor's skeleton.
An enzyme that turns a prenyl diphosphate into a terpene skeleton. Its gene sets a plant's scent; one broken basil synthase changes linalool into geraniol.
A large family of oxidising enzymes. In plants they decorate terpene skeletons (thymol, ursolic acid); in the liver they metabolise drugs and can bioactivate toxins.
The liver and gut P450 enzyme that metabolises about half of prescription drugs; inhibiting it can raise drug levels.
The route from phosphoenolpyruvate and erythrose 4-phosphate to the aromatic amino acids; at least 30 % of fixed carbon in vascular plants passes through it.
An enzyme that adds a methyl group to an oxygen. Two basil OMTs make estragole and methyleugenol; one amino acid decides which.
The largest class of plant natural products, built from five-carbon units; includes the essential-oil molecules, carnosic acid and ursolic acid.
A ten-carbon terpenoid; the main class of herb essential oils (menthol, thymol, linalool, 1,8-cineole, camphor, thujone).
A monoterpene carrying a C=O group, such as thujone, camphor, menthone and pulegone; several are the constituents of concern.
A fifteen-carbon terpenoid, made mainly in the cytosol: β-caryophyllene, α-bisabolol, chamazulene.
A sesquiterpene with a lactone ring; common in the Asteraceae and a frequent cause of contact allergy.
A twenty-carbon terpenoid: carnosic acid and carnosol in rosemary and sage; teucrin A (a clerodane) in germander.
A thirty-carbon terpenoid such as ursolic acid; waxy, insoluble in water and found in leaf surface wax.
A compound derived from phenylalanine via cinnamic acid: eugenol, estragole, methyleugenol, caffeic and rosmarinic acid.
A small acid carrying a phenol ring, such as caffeic acid; rosmarinic acid is an ester of two of them. Water-soluble, so well extracted into tea.
Loose term for plant compounds with several phenol rings (phenolic acids, flavonoids, tannins). Many are water-soluble; many are poorly absorbed.
A class of phenolics built from a phenylpropanoid unit plus three malonyl units: flavones, flavanones and more. Pigments, UV screens and signals in plants.
A subclass of flavonoids including apigenin, luteolin and the skullcap compounds baicalein and wogonin.
A flavonoid subclass without the 2,3 double bond of flavones; eriocitrin, peppermint tea's dominant phenolic, is a flavanone glycoside.
A molecule with a sugar attached (a glucoside if the sugar is glucose). The sugar makes flavonoids water-soluble; it must be removed before absorption.
A molecule joined to glucuronic acid. Plants make some (baicalin, wogonoside, scutellarin); the human liver and gut make many more to excrete compounds.
The non-sugar part of a glycoside: apigenin is the aglycone of apigenin-7-glucoside, baicalein of baicalin.
Both a class of benzopyrone compounds (herniarin, umbelliferone) and one specific molecule, coumarin. The anticoagulant and liver cautions concern the specific molecule.
A compound with several carbon-carbon triple bonds; chamomile's spiroethers belong here.
A colourless precursor, such as matricin in chamomile, that turns into a blue azulene when heated in steam distillation.
A blue aromatic hydrocarbon skeleton; chamazulene, formed from matricin during distillation, gives chamomile oil its colour.
The volatile, fragrant fraction of a plant recovered by steam distillation: mostly monoterpenes, sesquiterpenes and phenylpropenes.
Passing steam through plant material and condensing it; the volatile oil separates from the water. It is how essential oils are made, and heat can create new molecules.
Pouring hot water on plant material and letting it stand: a tea. It extracts water-soluble compounds well and volatile oil poorly.
Simmering plant material (usually roots or bark) in water, rather than steeping; longer and hotter than an infusion.
An extract made by soaking plant material in a mixture of ethanol and water. It reaches less polar compounds than water alone.
Made with a mixture of water and ethanol, such as a tincture or a 30-60 % ethanol extract.
How much plant went into how much finished extract, e.g. 1:5. It sets concentration but says nothing on its own about which compounds were extracted.
How unevenly a molecule's electric charge is spread. Polar molecules (sugars, glycosides) dissolve in water; non-polar ones (terpenes) in oils and less-polar solvents.
How much of a substance dissolves in a solvent at a given temperature; menthol is almost insoluble in water, glycosides dissolve readily.
How readily a substance evaporates. Volatile oil molecules escape from hot water and from drying leaves; phenolics do not.
The share of a compound or fraction in the plant that ends up in the preparation, e.g. 31 % of lemon balm oil reaching the tea.
A rate law in which the amount still to be extracted falls exponentially with time: fast at first, then levelling off.
A capsule coated to survive stomach acid and release its contents in the intestine; the form of peppermint oil tested for irritable bowel symptoms.
A protein that a signalling molecule binds to, triggering a response in the cell; the named molecular target of a compound.
A molecule that binds a receptor and activates it, as menthol activates the cold receptor TRPM8.
A molecule that binds a receptor or channel and blocks its activation, as α-thujone blocks the GABA-A receptor's chloride channel.
The brain's main inhibitory ion channel, opened by GABA. Thujone blocks it (convulsant); benzodiazepines bind a separate site on it.
An ion channel in sensory nerves that opens at cool temperatures and when menthol binds; why mint feels cold.
A cannabinoid receptor found mainly on immune cells; β-caryophyllene binds it selectively in laboratory studies.
Organic anion-transporting polypeptides: transporters that carry drugs such as statins into liver cells. Baicalin altered rosuvastatin exposure via OATP1B1.
The fraction of an ingested compound that reaches the bloodstream unchanged. Many plant polyphenols have very low bioavailability.
Metabolism of a swallowed compound by the gut wall and liver before it reaches general circulation; it can remove most of a dose.
When one substance changes the effect or blood level of another, e.g. by inhibiting the enzyme or transporter that handles it.
A multi-herb Japanese kampo formula containing S. baicalensis root; linked to interstitial pneumonitis and liver injury reports.
A compound with a known hazard or a regulatory threshold (thujone, pulegone, estragole, methyleugenol). Always curated, regardless of abundance.
Damage to the liver caused by a chemical. Reported for germander (teucrin A), pulegone and some skullcap products.
Conversion of a harmless-looking compound into a reactive, toxic one by the body's own enzymes, often cytochrome P450.
Able to damage DNA, for example by forming DNA adducts. A genotoxic carcinogen is assumed to have no fully safe threshold.
Causes cancer in rats or mice at the doses tested. Estragole and methyleugenol are rodent carcinogens; that is a hazard, not a measured human risk.
Substitution or contamination of a herbal product with another plant. Some liver injury blamed on skullcap was traced to germander.
Teucrium, a mint-family genus whose diterpenoid teucrin A causes liver injury; a known adulterant of skullcap.
An allergy to one substance causing reactions to related ones: ragweed-allergic people may react to chamomile.
A severe, rapid, whole-body allergic reaction that can be fatal; rare reports exist with chamomile.
A substance that causes an allergic skin reaction where it touches; carnosol is a major rosemary contact allergen.
Able to cause seizures. Thujone and camphor are convulsant at high doses; the EMA thujone limit is based on rodent seizure data.
A reflex stop in breathing (with spasm of the larynx) that menthol near the face can trigger in infants; why menthol oils are contraindicated under 2 years.
A condition in which a product should not be used, as stated in a monograph, e.g. hypersensitivity or age under 2 years for menthol oils.
The convulsant monoterpenoid ketone of sage (two isomers, α and β); blocks the GABA-A receptor. EMA sets daily exposure values for it.
A monoterpenoid ketone of mints that is hepatotoxic after bioactivation; limited by the EMA together with menthofuran.
A furan-containing monoterpene in peppermint oil and a major metabolite of pulegone; counted with pulegone under the EMA limit.
The aniseed-scented phenylpropene of some basils; a genotoxic carcinogen in rodents with an EMA guidance value of 0.05 mg per person per day.
A clove-like phenylpropene in most basil cultivars grown here; a rodent genotoxic carcinogen. The EMA gives no number but advises minimising exposure.
A chemically distinct form within one species, e.g. thymol-type versus other thyme, or estragole-rich versus linalool-rich basil. Same plant name, different oil.
A common gut disorder of abdominal pain and altered bowel habit; the condition in the peppermint-oil capsule trials.
A condition of persistent excessive worry; the population of the chamomile-extract trials.
